title: Integers & Number Properties
weightage: High — number-property facts underlie a large share of Quantitative Comparison and word-problem questions
intro: Number properties are the grammar of GRE Quant. The section almost never asks you to compute something hard; instead it asks whether a statement about integers is always true, and the winners are the people who know the rules of signs, parity (odd/even), and the peculiar behaviour of 0 and 1 cold. This chapter is the one place where memorising a short list of rules pays off on nearly every test, because those rules turn slow arithmetic into instant reasoning. Master them and you can answer many Quantitative Comparison questions without computing a single value — you simply decide what the sign or the parity of an expression must be.

topics.name: Integers, Signs & the Number Line
topics.details: An integer is a whole number with no fractional part: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, … . Note what is not an integer — 2.5, 3/4 and √2 are numbers but not integers, and the GRE deliberately blurs "number" and "integer" to bait you. The number line orders every real number from left (smaller) to right (larger), so −7 < −2 even though 7 > 2; on the negative side, the bigger the digit, the smaller the value. Distance on the line is always positive and equals the absolute difference |a − b|. Zero is an integer, is neither positive nor negative, and sits exactly between the two sides. When a GRE question says "x is a number" without saying "integer", you must allow fractions and negatives — that single word changes the answer to many Quantitative Comparison items.

solved.problem: List the integers strictly between −3.5 and 2.
solved.solution: Integers greater than −3.5 and less than 2: −3, −2, −1, 0, 1. That is 5 integers. (2 is excluded because "strictly between" is open.)

solved.problem: On the number line, which is greater: −8 or −3?
solved.solution: −3 lies to the RIGHT of −8, so −3 > −8. On the negative side the number closer to zero is larger.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: the distance between −5 and 6 on the number line. Quantity B: 10. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Distance = |6 − (−5)| = |11| = 11. Quantity A (11) > Quantity B (10), so Quantity A is greater.

solved.problem: How many integers x satisfy −4 ≤ x < 3?
solved.solution: x can be −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 — that is 7 values. (Include −4 because of ≤; exclude 3 because of <.)

unsolved.problem: How many integers lie strictly between −2 and 5?
What is the distance between −12 and −4 on the number line?

topics.name: Odd, Even & Consecutive Integers
topics.details: Parity is the single most tested number-property idea on the GRE. An even integer is any multiple of 2 (including 0 and negatives like −6); an odd integer leaves remainder 1 on division by 2. The rules are worth memorising as reflexes: even ± even = even, odd ± odd = even, odd ± even = odd; any product touching an even factor is even, and only odd × odd stays odd. Consecutive integers alternate parity, so among any 2 consecutive integers exactly one is even, and among any n consecutive integers the product is always divisible by n! (for example, the product of 3 consecutive integers is divisible by 6). A frequent trap: "the sum of two integers is even" does not tell you they are both even — they could both be odd. Test both possibilities before you commit.

solved.problem: If n is an integer, is n(n + 1) always even?
solved.solution: n and n + 1 are consecutive, so one of them is even. A product with an even factor is even. Yes — n(n + 1) is always even.

solved.problem: The sum of 5 consecutive integers is 5 times what?
solved.solution: Five consecutive integers are m−2, m−1, m, m+1, m+2 with middle m. Their sum is 5m, i.e. 5 times the middle (median) term. So the sum is always a multiple of 5.

solved.problem: If x is odd and y is even, what is the parity of 3x + 2y?
solved.solution: 3x = odd × odd = odd. 2y = even. odd + even = odd. So 3x + 2y is odd.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. x and y are integers with x + y odd. Quantity A: x·y. Quantity B: an even number. Which is greater / relationship?
solved.solution: If x + y is odd, one of x, y is even and the other odd, so their product x·y is even. Quantity A is even, matching Quantity B's parity — but the actual values are unknown, so the relationship cannot be determined.

unsolved.problem: If a is even and b is odd, what is the parity of a + b + 1?
The product of three consecutive integers is always divisible by what number?
hints: One factor is a multiple of 3.

unsolved.problem: If n is odd, is n² + n even or odd?
The sum of two integers is 21 (odd). Can both be even?
Four consecutive integers start at n. Is their sum even or odd?

topics.name: Positive/Negative Rules
topics.details: Signs behave predictably, and the GRE exploits every student who forgets that. For multiplication and division: same signs give a positive result, opposite signs give a negative; an even number of negative factors is positive, an odd number is negative. Powers follow the same logic — a negative base raised to an even power is positive, to an odd power is negative, so (−2)⁴ = 16 but (−2)³ = −8. The subtle traps live in inequalities: multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative reverses it, and a variable "number" may be negative, zero, or a fraction unless you are told otherwise. On Quantitative Comparison, plugging in a negative or a fraction (not just 2 or 3) is often what exposes a "cannot be determined" answer.

solved.problem: Evaluate (−3)² and −3².
solved.solution: (−3)² = (−3)(−3) = 9 (the negative is squared). But −3² means −(3²) = −9 (the power binds before the sign). They differ — read parentheses carefully.

solved.problem: What is the sign of (−1)(−2)(−3)(4)?
solved.solution: Count the negative factors: three of them (odd). An odd number of negatives is negative. The value is −24.

solved.problem: If −2x > 6, solve for x.
solved.solution: Divide both sides by −2 and FLIP the inequality: x < −3.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. x < 0. Quantity A: x³. Quantity B: x². Which is greater?
solved.solution: For any negative x, x³ is negative and x² is positive. A positive is always greater than a negative, so Quantity B is greater.

unsolved.problem: What is the sign of the product of five negative numbers?
If a > 0 and b < 0, what is the sign of a/b?

topics.name: Absolute Value
topics.details: The absolute value |x| is the distance of x from 0 on the number line, so it is never negative: |−7| = 7 and |7| = 7. Read it as "how far", not "which side". Two consequences drive most GRE questions. First, |x| = a (with a > 0) has two solutions, x = a and x = −a, so equations with absolute value usually branch. Second, |x − c| is the distance between x and c, which turns range statements into geometry: |x − 4| < 3 means x is within 3 of 4, i.e. 1 < x < 7. Basic rules: |x·y| = |x|·|y| and |x|² = x². The number-one mistake is treating |x| as "make it positive" — for a variable you must consider both signs, and on Quantitative Comparison that second case is often exactly where "cannot be determined" hides.

solved.problem: Solve |x − 2| = 5.
solved.solution: Distance 5 from 2 in both directions: x − 2 = 5 gives x = 7; x − 2 = −5 gives x = −3. Solutions: x = 7 or x = −3.

solved.problem: Solve |2x + 1| < 7.
solved.solution: Rewrite as −7 < 2x + 1 < 7. Subtract 1: −8 < 2x < 6. Divide by 2: −4 < x < 3.

solved.problem: If |x| = |−4|, what are the possible values of x?
solved.solution: |−4| = 4, so |x| = 4, giving x = 4 or x = −4.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: |−6| + |−2|. Quantity B: |−6 + (−2)|. Which is greater?
solved.solution: A = 6 + 2 = 8. B = |−8| = 8. They are equal — a reminder that |a| + |b| equals |a + b| only when a and b share a sign.

unsolved.problem: How many integer solutions does |x| < 3 have?

topics.name: Properties of Zero & One
topics.details: Zero and one carry special rules the GRE loves to test at the edges. Zero is an integer and is even, but it is neither positive nor negative; anything times 0 is 0; 0 divided by any nonzero number is 0; but division by 0 is undefined — a fast way the test creates "cannot be determined" traps. For exponents, any nonzero number to the 0 power is 1, and 0 to a positive power is 0 (0⁰ is not tested). One is the multiplicative identity (x·1 = x) and 1 raised to any power stays 1, while −1 alternates: (−1)^even = 1, (−1)^odd = −1. Also remember 1 is not prime. When a problem allows a denominator or a divisor to be a variable, always ask "could it be zero?" — that question alone resolves many Quantitative Comparison items.

solved.problem: Is 0 even, odd, or neither?
solved.solution: 0 is a multiple of 2 (0 = 2 × 0), so 0 is even. It is, however, neither positive nor negative.

solved.problem: Evaluate 7⁰ + 0⁵.
solved.solution: Any nonzero base to the 0 power is 1, so 7⁰ = 1. 0 to a positive power is 0, so 0⁵ = 0. Sum = 1.

solved.problem: For which value of x is the expression 5/(x − 3) undefined?
solved.solution: A fraction is undefined when its denominator is 0. x − 3 = 0 gives x = 3. So it is undefined at x = 3.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. x is a nonzero number. Quantity A: x⁰. Quantity B: 1. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Any nonzero number to the 0 power equals 1, so Quantity A = 1 = Quantity B. They are equal (the "nonzero" condition is what makes this safe).

shortcuts: On "is it always true?" questions, test small special cases in this order: 0, 1, −1, a fraction, a large number. One of them usually breaks a false claim.
Parity beats arithmetic: to check an answer, compute the odd/even of an expression instead of the value — it is faster and catches sign slips.
A product of n consecutive integers is divisible by n! (2 in a row → by 2, 3 in a row → by 6, 4 in a row → by 24).
To reverse an inequality you must multiply or divide by a negative — the on-screen calculator will not warn you, so flag the flip yourself.
|x − c| is "distance from c". Turn every absolute-value inequality into a distance statement and read the range off the number line.
When a denominator or divisor is a variable, immediately ask "can it be 0?" — that single check resolves many Quantitative Comparison traps.
mistakes: Assuming a "number" is a positive integer. Unless told so, it may be negative, zero, or a fraction — the source of most "cannot be determined" answers.
Writing −3² = 9. Without parentheses the exponent binds first: −3² = −9, while (−3)² = 9.
Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Solving |x| = a with only one answer. It gives two: x = a and x = −a (when a > 0).
Calling 1 prime, or forgetting that 0 is even. Both cost easy points on definition questions.
Treating |a + b| as |a| + |b|. They are equal only when a and b have the same sign.

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — x is an integer. Quantity A: x². Quantity B: x. Which is greater?
pyq.a: Cannot be determined. For x = 2, A > B; for x = 1, they are equal; for x = 0, equal; the fractional/negative cases the GRE wants you to test change the outcome, so no single relationship holds.

pyq.q: A question states "n is a positive even integer". Why does that wording matter?
pyq.a: It removes 0, negatives and fractions from play, so parity rules apply cleanly. The GRE adds or omits each of those three words on purpose — read them like part of the equation.

pyq.q: Numeric Entry — the product of three consecutive integers is 210. Enter the largest of the three.
pyq.a: 5 × 6 × 7 = 210, so the integers are 5, 6, 7 and the largest is 7. (Use divisibility by 6 to narrow the search quickly.)

pyq.q: Multiple-answer — which of these must be even for every integer n? Select all: n²+n, 2n+1, n(n−1), 3n.
pyq.a: n²+n = n(n+1) is even, and n(n−1) is even (both are products of consecutive integers). 2n+1 is always odd; 3n has the parity of n. So the even-for-all choices are n²+n and n(n−1).

summary: Integers are whole numbers; watch for the word "integer" vs "number" — it decides whether fractions and negatives are allowed.
Parity rules (odd/even) let you answer many questions without computing a value.
Signs: same-sign products are positive, an odd count of negatives is negative, and negative bases flip sign only on odd powers.
Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative reverses it.
|x| is distance from 0: |x| = a branches into two cases, and |x − c| reads as a range on the number line.
0 is even and neither positive nor negative; division by 0 is undefined; x⁰ = 1 for x ≠ 0; 1 is not prime.
Products of consecutive integers are highly divisible — n in a row is divisible by n!.
On Quantitative Comparison, test 0, 1, −1 and a fraction before deciding; "cannot be determined" is a real answer.
